question: A 58-year-old man with known peptic ulcer disease and eGFR of 55 mL/min (CKD Stage G3a) presents with moderate knee pain from osteoarthritis. Which analgesic strategy is most appropriate as first-line therapy?

answers.text: Oral diclofenac 50 mg three times daily — most potent NSAID for degenerative joint pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diclofenac is absolutely contraindicated in this patient: peptic ulcer disease (GI risk) AND CKD G3a (nephrotoxicity risk from reduced renal prostaglandin synthesis). NSAIDs are inappropriate here.

answers.text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) 1 g up to four times daily with activity modification and physiotherapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For degenerative joint pain in a patient with active peptic ulcer disease and CKD, paracetamol is the safest first-line analgesic. It has no GI mucosal toxicity, no nephrotoxic mechanism, and is effective for mild-to-moderate degenerative pain when combined with non-pharmacological measures.

answers.text: Celecoxib 200 mg once daily with a proton-pump inhibitor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: COX-2 selective inhibitors (celecoxib) reduce GI mucosal risk but retain nephrotoxic effects equivalent to non-selective NSAIDs. Celecoxib is still contraindicated in significant CKD (eGFR < 60 is a relative contraindication; < 30 is absolute).

answers.text: Tramadol 50 mg twice daily as a safer alternative to NSAIDs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tramadol is an opioid with serotonergic and adrenergic activity. While it avoids GI and renal prostaglandin concerns, it is not first-line for degenerative joint pain. Paracetamol plus physiotherapy should be tried first.

overallFeedback.feedback: With peptic ulcer disease AND CKD G3a, all NSAIDs — including COX-2 selective — are contraindicated or to be avoided. Paracetamol is the correct first-line choice.
Well done. Paracetamol is the safest and most appropriate first-line analgesic when NSAIDs are contraindicated due to peptic ulcer disease and CKD.
